title: Denim Art That Unpacks American Myths
summary: Have you ever thought about what your jeans really mean? Artist Nick Doyle has, and he's turned denim into huge wall sculptures that tell stories about America. He uses layers of denim to create things like sunglasses reflecting clouds, a mountain landscape, and even a life-sized fortune teller's shop. Denim isn't just fabric to Doyle. It's a symbol of American culture—from cowboys and gold rushes to the tough guys like James Dean. But it also has a darker history, because enslaved people used to dye cotton with indigo. Doyle found his first roll of denim in the trash in 2018, and it sparked a whole new way of making art. His show, called Collective Hallucinations, is at the Perrotin gallery in New York City until May 30. If you're in town, go check it out. You'll never look at your jeans the same way again!
why_it_matters: Your jeans might seem ordinary, but learning the hidden stories behind everyday objects helps you think critically about where things come from and how your country's history shapes everyday life.

background_read: Denim originally came from a French fabric called 'serge de Nîmes', and it became popular during the California Gold Rush when miners needed sturdy pants.
James Dean (a famous actor from the 1950s) made jeans a symbol of teenage coolness in movies like 'Rebel Without a Cause'.
The blue color often came from indigo, which was grown and processed by enslaved Africans in the American South, linking denim to both pride and painful history.

Nick Doyle (a contemporary American artist) turns this everyday material into wall-sized art at Perrotin gallery (a well-known art gallery founded in Paris) to explore big ideas about the United States.
Article_Structure: WHAT: Creates oversized denim sculptures that examine American myths
WHERE: Displayed at the Perrotin gallery in New York City until May 30
WHY: Because he sees denim as a symbol of both American triumphs and its darker history, like the use of enslaved people to dye cotton

perspectives.description: Doyle's art makes viewers see denim as more than just clothing, opening a thoughtful conversation about culture.
Some people may feel the artwork focuses too much on the negative parts of history and not enough on the positive.
Art often uses familiar materials to make us question and learn, and it's up to each person what they take away from it.
